word_order: SOV — verbs and predicates consistently appear at clause end (e.g. '가는 목적이 있어가지고', '3번밖에 안 탔다는 거야')
punctuation_present: sometimes — some sentences end with '.', '?' while many transcribed utterances trail off with no mark or end mid-connector
register: spontaneous informal spoken conversation (casual dialogue/interview transcript with hesitations and self-correction)
non_boundary_traps: trailing '-가지고' or '-다 보니까' (incomplete, speaker will continue)
fillers like '이제', '그', '막' that resemble discourse openers but carry no boundary
target_language_risks: Pro-drop: subjects/objects often omitted, so a segment alone may lack a clear English subject
Verb-final structure means core meaning (verb, negation, tense, mood) only resolves at clause end — early segmentation risks mistranslating clause type (statement vs question vs quote)
Sentence-final particles (거든, 잖아, 는데) encode nuance/mood not directly translatable without following context
Unfinished/trailing utterances (ending in -아서/어서, -가지고) leave semantic completion pending, risking fragment translations that read as complete false sentences
Frequent self-repair and repeated fillers can be mistaken for content words if not filtered
notes_for_prompt_writer: Segment primarily at sentence-final punctuation or clear sentence-final verb endings (-어, -네, -더라, -거야) rather than at every connective suffix, since -는데/-고/-어서/-니까 usually continue rather than end a clause. Treat fillers (어, 음, 이제, 그, 막) as non-boundary noise to be skipped, not segment starters. Because Korean is SOV and pro-drop, delay commitment on subject/object identity until the verb is seen, and be cautious with clauses trailing off (ending in -아서/어서/가지고) as they signal continuation into the next utterance.
